\section[cakram]{\sk{चक्रम्} (cakram) — a wheel}

\label{lesson:SA-C41-wheel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{modakaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{चक्रम्}}
\textbf{\sk{चक्रम्}} (\emph{cakram}) — \textquotedblleft{}a wheel\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{चक्रम्}} is a wheel, a disc, a circle of anything.

It is an old root for turning, \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}el-}, said twice — and the same doubling gives Greek \emph{kuklos}, which English keeps in \emph{cycle} and \emph{cyclone}. English \emph{wheel} is the same word by the Germanic road.

English later borrowed the Sanskrit itself, unworn, as \emph{chakra}, so the word now sits in the language twice over.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A wheel, and a root that turns in three languages at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cakram}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{modakaḥ}, then \emph{cakram}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{चक्रम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a wheel\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kalaśaḥ]{\sk{कलशः} (kalaśaḥ) — a water-pot}

\label{lesson:SA-C41-pot}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{cakram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कलशः}}
\textbf{\sk{कलशः}} (\emph{kalaśaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a water-pot\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{कलशः}} is the round-bellied water-pot — the one set at a \sk{द्वारम्} with leaves and a coconut on top, and any pot of that shape.

Fill it with \sk{पानीयम्} and it is doing its everyday job; put it at a doorway and it is doing its other one.

Greek \emph{kalux}, a husk or a cup, has been offered as a cousin, and Latin \emph{calix}, which English keeps in \emph{chalice}, names the same swelling shape.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pot that holds water and welcomes people.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kalaśaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cakram}, then \emph{kalaśaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{कलशः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a water-pot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[plavaḥ]{\sk{प्लवः} (plavaḥ) — a boat, a raft}

\label{lesson:SA-C41-boat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{kalaśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्लवः}}
\textbf{\sk{प्लवः}} (\emph{plavaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a boat, a raft\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{प्लवः}} is a boat, and more exactly a float — a raft, a hull, anything that swims rather than sinks.

From \emph{plu}, \textquotedblleft{}to float, to swim\textquotedblright{}, and the family is enormous: Greek \emph{plein}, \textquotedblleft{}to sail\textquotedblright{}, Latin \emph{pluere}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{}, English \emph{flow}, \emph{float} and \emph{fleet}.

Where there is no \sk{सेतुः} across the \sk{नदी}, there is a \textbf{\sk{प्लवः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
What carries you over when there is no bridge.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{plavaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kalaśaḥ}, then \emph{plavaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{प्लवः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a boat, a raft\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[darpaṇaḥ]{\sk{दर्पणः} (darpaṇaḥ) — a mirror}

\label{lesson:SA-C41-mirror}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{plavaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दर्पणः}}
\textbf{\sk{दर्पणः}} (\emph{darpaṇaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mirror\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{दर्पणः}} is a mirror — a disc of metal polished bright, centuries before glass could do the job.

It stands on \emph{dṛp}, \textquotedblleft{}to be proud\textquotedblright{}, so the object is named for what people do in front of it rather than for what it is made of. That is a small joke three thousand years old.

Hindi \emph{darpaṇ} is the same word, unchanged.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A mirror, named for vanity rather than for glass.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{darpaṇaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{plavaḥ}, then \emph{darpaṇaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{दर्पणः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mirror\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chatram]{\sk{छत्रम्} (chatram) — a parasol}

\label{lesson:SA-C41-parasol}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{plavaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{darpaṇaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{छत्रम्}}
\textbf{\sk{छत्रम्}} (\emph{chatram}) — \textquotedblleft{}a parasol\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{छत्रम्}} is a parasol: the shade held over a \emph{rājā}, and the umbrella carried in the rain.

From \emph{chad}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{}. The covering is the whole of it — what the \textbf{\sk{छत्रम्}} covers you from, sun or water, the word does not say.

It went east as well as up in the world: Hindi \emph{chātā}, the umbrella anyone carries, is this word worn smooth.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things made by hand: a wheel, a pot, a boat, a mirror, a parasol.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chatram}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{cakram} and \emph{chatram} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{छत्रम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a parasol\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
